identity.title: VLT/SPHERE- and ALMA-based shape reconstruction of asteroid (3) Juno

paper_type_evidence.quote: We use the recently released Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) and VLT/SPHERE science verification data, together with earlier adaptive-optics images, stellar occultation, and lightcurve data

redshift_or_distance.value: Range to observer 1.12-2.41 au for the AO epochs (Table 1); ALMA resolution 0.021'' ~ 30 km projected

evidence.quote: despite its large diameter of about 250 km

question.value: Can the 3D shape and spin of asteroid (3) Juno be reconstructed from ALMA visibilities combined with AO images and lightcurves, and what does the shape imply about non-gravitational features?

evidence.quote: allows us, for the first time, to explore the viability of the shape reconstruction of asteroids from disk-resolved thermal infrared observations.
ADS/JAO.ALMA#2011.0.00013.SV
At the observed frequencies of 224, 226, 240, and 242 GHz
thereby providing projected baselines between 26 m and 13 km.
angular resolutions as high as 0.021 ′′, or about 30 km projected at the distance of Juno.

time_on_source.value: ten epochs over 4.4 h; each epoch 18 min

evidence.quote: A total of ten different epochs spread over 4.4 h were acquired
each epoch on Juno lasted for 18 min, during which time Juno rotated 15 ◦.
Juno was observed with ALMA on 2014 Oct. 19 using between 27 and 33 antennas

provided.value: Science verification AO images of Juno

evidence.quote: We used the classical imaging mode of SPHERE (IRDIS, Dohlen et al. 2008) to image the apparent disk of Juno.

other_facilities.name: Keck NIRC2, VLT NACO, Mt. Wilson ADOPT
Pic-du-Midi 1 m telescope and archival lightcurves

evidence.quote: we acquired a lightcurve in April 2015 at the 1 m telescope of the Pic-du-Midi Observatory, France.
only the occultation from 1979 with 16 full chords can be used for recovering an almost complete silhouette

what.value: Mt. Wilson ADOPT AO images taken directly from the paper

evidence.quote: The original data were no longer available in a usable format, so we used the images directly from the paper.

what.value: 11 diameter and 23 mass estimates of Juno

evidence.quote: There are 11 diameter and 23 mass estimates for (3) Juno in the literature (see Appendix)

what.value: Thermal inertia of Juno 5 J m-2 s-0.5 K-1

evidence.quote: owing to the very low thermal inertia of Juno of 5 J m −2 s −0.5 K −1 (Mueller & Lagerros 1998)

evidence.quote: We used the calibrated visibility data instead of the ALMA deconvolved images

evidence.quote: The model reconstructed from the self-calibrated, deconvolved images instead of the raw data revealed no additional detail
We used the ADAM algorithm (Viikinkoski & Kaasalainen 2014; Viikinkoski et al. 2015) for the shape and spin reconstruction.

what.value: ALMA data reduction and self-calibration of the SV data

evidence.quote: As stated by ALMA Partnership et al. (2015), each epoch on Juno lasted for 18 min

what.value: Averaging of literature diameters by sigma rejection

evidence.quote: following the method by Carry et al. (2012)

Data weighting between ALMA, AO and lightcurve terms and regularization weights in ADAM

method.value: Calibrated ALMA visibilities, deconvolved AO images, lightcurves; occultation used only as check

evidence.quote: the ALMA visibility data were combined with disk-integrated photometry and with the adaptive-optics images, and checked against the occultation data.

key_parameters.value: Mt. Wilson image scale a free parameter

evidence.quote: we included it in the optimization as a free parameter.

method.value: ADAM with octantoid and subdivision-surface shape supports; semi-analytical FFT-based thermal model

evidence.quote: We used both subdivision surfaces and octantoid parametrization for shape representations
we used a simple, semi-analytical FFT-based approach

assumptions.value: Low thermal inertia of 5 J m-2 s-0.5 K-1

evidence.quote: owing to the very low thermal inertia of Juno of 5 J m −2 s −0.5 K −1

validation.value: Compared different shape supports and data subsets; occultation consistency check; self-calibration test

evidence.quote: we checked the effect of data sources by observing the model variations under varying data subset combinations.

method.value: Compare diameter with literature mass average to get density and porosity versus L chondrite grain density

evidence.quote: Using this estimate, we find a density of 3.32 ± 0.40 g cm −3.
Compared with the grain density of L ordinary chondrites (Consolmagno et al. 2008)

used_for.value: All-data asteroid modelling of shape and spin

evidence.quote: model the 3D shape and spin of the large asteroid (3) Juno with the all-data asteroid modelling (ADAM) procedure

used_for.value: Deconvolution of NACO, NIRC2 and SPHERE images

evidence.quote: unlike Mistral (Mugnier et al. 2004), the algorithm we used to deconvolve the images from NACO, NIRC2, and SPHERE
Our determination of 249 ± 5 km corresponds exactly to this average diameter.
we find a density of 3.32 ± 0.40 g cm −3.
this implies a porosity of 7 ± 1%
an average mass of 2.68 ± 0.24 × 10 19 kg

findings_qualitative.value: Juno has sizable unrounded features likely from impacts, in the transition between dwarf planets and medium asteroids

evidence.quote: Its global shape features are apparently molded by other than gravitational processes (likely impacts).

claims.hypothesis: Shapes of asteroids can be reconstructed from raw ALMA visibilities combined with other data
claims.experiment: ADAM fit to ALMA visibilities, lightcurves and AO images
claims.result: Model with D = 249 ± 5 km, consistent with occultation
claims.finding: Reconstruction is viable and shape is robust to variations

evidence.quote: Different and independent shape supports and regularization methods generate similar shapes

claims.hypothesis: Juno is not fully rounded despite its size
claims.experiment: Compared shapes from two supports and data subsets

evidence.quote: Juno has sizable unrounded features moulded by non-gravitational processes such as impacts.

claims.hypothesis: ALMA self-calibration matters for the shape
claims.finding: Not a major concern at this resolution

evidence.quote: so the self-calibration is not a major concern here.

why_this_method.value: Raw visibilities avoid information loss and distortion from CLEAN and self-calibration

evidence.quote: The “clean” ALMA images obtained by various deconvolution and self-calibration processes inevitably lose and distort some of the original information.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Mt. Wilson features not fully accommodated; occultation data used only as check

evidence.quote: The last did not improve the reliability of the solution or provide more information

limitations_admitted.value: Northern hemisphere less constrained due to southern-only viewing geometry

evidence.quote: so the northern parts of the model are less constrained.

limitations_admitted.value: Residual antenna phase errors may exist in raw ALMA data

evidence.quote: there usually are residual antennabased phase errors in the raw ALMA data (Hezaveh et al. 2013).

referee_caveats_inferred: No formal fit statistics or chi-square given for the ALMA data
Weights between data types not given
Uncertainties on shape not derived transparently

data_public_as_stated.value: ALMA SV data publicly released; model on DAMIT

evidence.quote: This model can be downloaded at the DAMIT web site.

reproducibility.score_reason: Public data and a published model exist, but the ADAM settings and weights are not given.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: The recipe depends on ADAM and unstated parameters.
